# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Nissaggiya Pācittiya 15 (Bu-Vb Np15)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Np15
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Nissaggiya Pācittiya 15
**Title (English, from literature):** Making an inappropriate sitting blanket
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin01m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

*Nisīdanasanthata* (Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Nissaggiya Pācittiya 15) sets out the Vinaya regulation concerning the manufacture of a sitting-mat or blanket (*nisīdanasanthata*). According to the rule, a bhikkhu who makes a new sitting-mat without incorporating a piece from an old blanket incurs an offense requiring forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and formal confession (*pācittiya*). The promulgation of the rule begins with a narrative setting that establishes foundational principles of monastic law, featuring an episode with the venerable Upasena [Rosen 1959]. An English translation of the text is available by Bhikkhu Brahmali.

The rule and its origin narrative are discussed in later Pali literature, specifically within the *Milindapañha* in the *Uttarikaraṇīyapañha* (Mil 5.1.9) and the *Dhutaṅgapañha* (Mil 6.4.2). DharmaNexus detects extensive text reuse with 113 other Pali works, sharing standard casuistic and Vinaya formulations with adjacent rules of the Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (especially Np 11, Np 12, Np 13, and Np 14), Khandhaka chapters such as the *Vattakkhandhaka* (Kd 18), *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), and *Kammakkhandhaka* (Kd 11), suttas in the *Ānāpāna Saṁyutta* (SN 54) and *Magga Saṁyutta* (SN 45), and the commentary *Pārājikakaṇḍa-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].

Pali Nissaggiya Pācittiya 15 corresponds directly to *Naiḥsargika-Pātayantika* rule 15 across other Buddhist traditions [Rosen 1959]. Curated parallels include the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and Parivāra in Pali, as well as canonical Prātimokṣa and Vinayavibhaṅga recensions preserved in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan belonging to the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Dharmaguptaka, Mahāsāṅghika, and Kāśyapīya traditions. Computational alignments from DharmaNexus confirm close matches with the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D0003-2), the *Vinaya-uttaragrantha* (D0007A), and related treatises such as the *Vinayasūtraṭīkā* (D4120) [DharmaNexus].
